entry.title: Introducing Jobic: A CMS built on Laravel
entry.summary: Meet JobMetric's flagship CMS for teams that want an editorial workspace and a Laravel application they can extend.
entry.content:
Jobic is JobMetric's flagship CMS. It gives editorial teams a workspace for managing content and gives developers a Laravel application they can extend with the same tools they already use.

A workspace for the people who run the site​

Editors can write pages and posts with a block editor, preview their drafts, and select assets from a shared media library. Teams working in multiple languages can manage active languages and edit language-specific content. Role-based permissions help teams give editors and administrators access to the work each role handles.

Laravel stays at the center​

The application still uses Eloquent for data, Blade for views, Laravel policies for authorization, and Artisan for command-line tasks. When your site needs a custom catalog, a member area, or an integration with another service, your developers can build it using those same conventions.

A publishing team might start with posts, media, and editorial review. A business might start with pages and add a catalog later. Both projects can use the same CMS foundation and grow in different directions.

Explore Jobic for a closer look at the workspace, architecture, and setup.

entry.title: From draft to publication with Jobic’s editorial workflows
entry.summary: See how Jobic combines the block editor, Kanban, role-based transitions, and workflow simulation.
entry.content:
Publishing gets harder when several people review a post, work across languages, or need to agree on when a draft is ready. Jobic brings that work together with an editor, a content Kanban board, and configurable workflow transitions.

Give each stage a purpose​

An author can write and preview a draft, then send it for review when the configured workflow allows it. The Kanban board helps the team see posts by stage. A reviewer can move a post through an available transition, subject to that person's role and the workflow's rules.

A simple workflow might have Draft, Review, and Publish stages. Teams can define stages and transitions around their own editorial process.

Test a workflow before using it with real content​

Jobic's workflow designer can simulate an unsaved workflow. Provide a sample draft, choose a stage and role, then inspect which transitions are available and which checks pass. The simulation does not publish the draft or execute workflow actions.

Start with one review step that solves a real problem for your team. Test it with two roles, such as author and reviewer, before adding more stages.

See the editorial workspace on the Jobic product page.

entry.title: The open-source Laravel packages behind Jobic
entry.summary: Meet the JobMetric packages that handle permissions, editorial workflows, and localization in Jobic.
entry.content:
Jobic brings several of JobMetric's open-source Laravel packages together in one application. You can also use those packages independently when your own Laravel project needs a single capability.

Three capabilities, separate packages​

  • Rolix gives Jobic a foundation for role-based permissions. Jobic uses it to enforce access to admin pages and actions.
  • Laravel Flow provides building blocks for stages and transitions. Jobic uses them to model how posts move through editorial review.
  • Laravel Language and Laravel Translation support language records and translatable fields. Jobic uses them in its multilingual content workflow.

This separation gives teams a practical choice. If your existing Laravel app needs workflow states, you can explore Laravel Flow on its own. If you want a CMS with an editorial workspace, media library, and role management, look at how Jobic brings those capabilities together.

Browse JobMetric’s package documentation or see how the packages fit into Jobic.
